title: CALCULUS 1
body:
Calculus is what you get when you take a limit of something you already know how to do. Slope is
rise over run, which needs two points; take the [[Limit]] as the two points merge and you get the
[[Derivative]], the slope at a single point. Area is base times height, which needs a rectangle;
take the limit of a [[Riemann Sum]] of skinny rectangles and you get the [[Integral]], the area
under a curve. Those are the only two ideas in the course, and the
[[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]] says they undo each other.

The reason this course matters for a CS degree is not the algebra, it is that **the derivative is
the answer to "which way should I move to make this smaller"**. That is the entire content of
[[Gradient Descent]], and [[Back Propagation]] is the [[Chain Rule]] applied through a stack of
layers. [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and the [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS|neural-network]] material are
downstream of this note by a shorter path than of anything else in the MATH block except
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA]]. The other reason is [[STATISTICS]]: a continuous [[Random Variable]] is
*defined* by an integral, so probability is an area and expectation is $\int x f(x)\,dx$.

The single organising idea, if you keep one: **calculus is local linear approximation.** The
derivative says what linear function best matches your curve at a point ([[Linear Approximation]]
makes that literal), and everything from [[Related Rates]] to [[Optimization]] to
[[Curve Sketching]] is that approximation being read for information.

## Topics

### Limits and continuity

- [[Limit]]: what $\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L$ means, one-sided limits, limits at infinity, the
  limit laws, and the indeterminate forms ($0/0$, $\infty/\infty$) that make the whole subject
  necessary
- [[Continuity]]: continuous at a point, continuous on an interval, the three ways it can fail,
  and the Intermediate Value Theorem, which is the first existence theorem in the degree

### The derivative

- [[Derivative]]: the limit of the difference quotient, secant lines converging on a tangent, and
  the three readings of one number (slope, instantaneous rate of change, sensitivity)
- [[Differentiation Rules]]: the table you memorise. Constant, power, constant multiple, sum,
  product, quotient, plus the transcendentals ($e^x$, $\ln x$, and the trig family)
- [[Chain Rule]]: differentiating a composition, and the one rule the rest of the degree actually
  uses
- [[Trigonometric Function]]: sine, cosine, and the rest as the functions whose derivatives cycle
  with period four
- [[Implicit Differentiation]]: differentiating an equation that was never solved for $y$, and
  where tangent lines to circles and ellipses come from

### Applications of the derivative

- [[Related Rates]]: two quantities tied by an equation, both changing in time, and you know one
  rate and want the other. The setup is the whole difficulty
- [[Linear Approximation]]: replacing $f$ near a point by its tangent line, and the differential
  $dy = f'(x)\,dx$ that the notation is built around
- [[Curve Sketching]]: critical points, the first and second derivative tests, concavity, and
  inflection points, all read off $f'$ and $f''$
- [[Optimization]]: finding the largest or smallest value a quantity can take. The closed-interval
  method, and the modelling step that turns a word problem into one variable
- [[Mean Value Theorem]]: the theoretical result that makes the derivative tests legal, and the
  reason "zero derivative everywhere means constant" is a theorem rather than an assumption

### Integration

- [[Integral]]: antiderivatives, indefinite versus definite, area under a curve, and the notation
- [[Riemann Sum]]: the limit-of-rectangles construction that the definite integral *is*, before
  anyone shows you a shortcut
- [[Fundamental Theorem of Calculus]]: both parts, and the reason integration is computable at
  all rather than a numerical exercise
- [[U-Substitution]]: the chain rule run backwards. The only technique in Calc 1;
  [[Integration Techniques|the rest]] belong to [[CALCULUS 2]]

## Core Facts to Know

- A [[Limit]] describes what $f(x)$ **approaches**, not what it equals. $f(a)$ can be anything or
  undefined and the limit is unaffected.
- The two-sided limit exists **iff** both one-sided limits exist and agree. This is the entire
  test for a jump discontinuity.
- $0/0$ is **indeterminate, not undefined**: it means "do more work", usually factor, rationalise,
  or divide by the highest power. $c/0$ with $c \neq 0$ is a vertical asymptote instead.
- $\lim_{x\to\infty} f(x)$ compares growth rates, which is the same question
  [[Asymptotic Analysis]] asks about algorithms with different notation.
- $\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{\sin x}{x} = 1$. Every trig derivative comes from it.
- Continuous at $a$ means three things at once: $f(a)$ exists, $\lim_{x\to a} f(x)$ exists, and
  they are equal.
- **Differentiable $\Rightarrow$ continuous, never the reverse.** $|x|$ at $0$ is the counterexample
  to keep: continuous, corner, no derivative.
- The Intermediate Value Theorem: a continuous function on $[a,b]$ hits every value between $f(a)$
  and $f(b)$. It proves a root exists; it does not find it. That is bisection search's warrant.
- $f'(x) = \lim_{h\to 0} \frac{f(x+h) - f(x)}{h}$. Everything else is a shortcut for this.
- $\frac{d}{dx}x^n = nx^{n-1}$, $\frac{d}{dx}e^x = e^x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\ln x = \frac{1}{x}$,
  $\frac{d}{dx}\sin x = \cos x$, $\frac{d}{dx}\cos x = -\sin x$.
- Product rule $(fg)' = f'g + fg'$. Quotient rule
  $\left(\frac{f}{g}\right)' = \frac{f'g - fg'}{g^2}$, **low d-high minus high d-low over low
  squared**, and the order matters because subtraction does not commute.
- **The derivative of a product is not the product of the derivatives.** Same for quotients. The
  sum rule is the only one that works the naive way.
- [[Chain Rule]]: $(f(g(x)))' = f'(g(x)) \cdot g'(x)$. Differentiate the outside, leave the inside
  alone, multiply by the derivative of the inside.
- Trig derivatives cycle with period 4: $\sin \to \cos \to -\sin \to -\cos \to \sin$. The ones
  starting with **c** get the minus sign.
- Implicit differentiation is just the chain rule with $y = y(x)$: every $y$ you differentiate
  spits out a $\frac{dy}{dx}$, then you solve for it.
- **A critical point is where $f'(x) = 0$ or $f'$ does not exist.** Not every critical point is an
  extremum ($x^3$ at $0$), which is why there is a second test.
- First derivative test: $f'$ changes $+ \to -$ means local max, $- \to +$ means local min. Second
  derivative test: $f''(c) > 0$ means min (holds water), $f''(c) < 0$ means max, $f''(c) = 0$ tells
  you **nothing**.
- $f'' > 0$ is concave up, $f'' < 0$ is concave down, and an inflection point is where concavity
  *changes*, which requires a sign change and not merely $f'' = 0$.
- **Extreme Value Theorem**: a continuous function on a **closed** interval attains an absolute max
  and min. On an open interval it need not. This is why the closed-interval method checks endpoints
  as well as critical points.
- [[Mean Value Theorem]]: on $[a,b]$ there is a $c$ where $f'(c) = \frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}$. Somewhere
  the instantaneous rate equals the average rate. Rolle's theorem is the case $f(a) = f(b)$.
- Linear approximation: $f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x-a)$. It is the degree-1 [[Taylor Series]]
  truncation, which is the same idea Calc 2 takes to $n$ terms.
- The **indefinite** integral is a family of functions and needs $+C$; the **definite** integral is
  a number and does not. Losing the $+C$ is the most common mark lost in the course.
- $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$ is a **signed** area. Area below the axis counts negative, so total area
  needs $|f|$ or a split at the roots.
- FTC Part 1: $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f(t)\,dt = f(x)$. Differentiation undoes integration.
- FTC Part 2: $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)$ for any antiderivative $F$. This is what makes a
  limit of infinitely many rectangles into a two-line subtraction.
- $u$-substitution is the chain rule backwards: pick $u$ to be the inside function, and
  $du = u'(x)\,dx$ has to consume the leftover factor or the substitution does not close. On a
  definite integral, **change the limits** or convert back before evaluating.
- $\int x^n dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C$ **except at $n = -1$**, where the answer is $\ln|x| + C$.
- Differentiation is mechanical and always works on elementary functions. Integration is not:
  $e^{-x^2}$ has no elementary antiderivative, which is exactly why the normal distribution's CDF
  in [[STATISTICS]] comes from a table.

## Related courses

- [[CALCULUS 2]] (MATH 2200) is the direct sequel and picks up exactly where
  [[U-Substitution]] stops: [[Integration Techniques]] takes over integration, and
  [[Infinite Series]] and [[Taylor Series]] generalise [[Linear Approximation]] from one term to
  infinitely many. [[Double Integral]] is where the area-under-a-curve picture stops being enough.
- [[MATHEMATICAL METHODS]] (MATH 3200) is the same material with more variables.
  [[Multivariable Calculus]] and [[Gradient]] are what [[Derivative]] becomes when the input is a
  vector, [[Multivariable Chain Rule]] is what [[Chain Rule]] becomes, and
  [[Differential Equations]] are what you get when the unknown is a function and the equation
  involves its derivatives.
- [[STATISTICS]] (MATH 2234) has this course as its stated prerequisite and it is not decorative.
  A [[Probability Density Function]] is a function whose [[Integral]] over everything is $1$, a
  probability is an area under it, the CDF is its antiderivative, and [[Average Value]] is the
  continuous version of a mean with the sum replaced by an integral. See [[Random Variable]].
- [[LINEAR ALGEBRA]] (MATH 1203): [[Trigonometric Function]] identities are what [[Polar Form]]
  runs on, and $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$ is where the two courses meet.
- [[FOURIER AND COMPLEX ANALYSIS]] (MATH 4199) takes the trig functions as a basis rather than as
  a family of formulas, and [[Fourier Series]] coefficients are integrals.
- [[MACHINE LEARNING]] and [[THE NEW TURING OMNIBUS]]: this is the course the neural-network
  material actually runs on. [[Gradient Descent]] is [[Optimization]] with more variables and no
  closed form, [[Back Propagation]] is the [[Chain Rule]] applied through a composition of layers,
  and a [[Loss Function]] is the thing being minimised. [[Least Squares]] and
  [[Linear Regression]] are the case where setting the derivative to zero still has an answer you
  can write down.
- [[INFORMATION STRUCTURES]] (COMP 2631): [[Asymptotic Analysis]] compares growth rates with
  limits at infinity, informally. $O$, $\Omega$, and $\Theta$ are limit statements about
  $f(n)/g(n)$, and [[Time Complexity]]'s ladder is the same ordering of functions this course
  builds when it does $\lim_{x\to\infty}$.
- [[COMPUTING MACHINERY 2]] (COMP 2659): [[Continuous]] there is signal vocabulary, the opposite
  of [[Discrete]]. [[Continuity]] here is the analytic property. One word, two subjects; see the
  note.
